segments.caption: Research papers love to say it: p is less than 0.05.
But what does a p-value actually mean? Let's make it simple.
Here's the definition, in simple words.
The p-value is the chance of getting results at least as extreme as yours, if nothing special were going on.
A small p-value means: this would be really surprising, by luck alone.
Back to the coin that landed heads 9 times out of 10.
If the coin were fair, 9 or 10 heads would happen just 1% of the time.
So the p-value is 0.01.
Now compare: 6 heads out of 10.
6 or more heads happens 38% of the time, so the p-value is 0.38.
Small p-value: hard to explain by luck. Big p-value: easily luck.
By convention, a p-value below 0.05 is called statistically significant.
But that line is a habit, not a law of nature. 0.049 and 0.051 are almost the same evidence.
Here's the most common mistake.
A p-value of 0.01 does not mean a 1% chance that the null is true.
It's the chance of the data if the null were true. Not the chance of the null, given the data.
And a tiny p-value doesn't mean a big effect.
With millions of users, even a tiny difference gets a tiny p-value. So always check how big the effect really is.
So remember: the p-value tells you how surprising your data would be, if nothing were going on.
Small means surprising. But it is not the chance that the null is true.
Quick quiz!
A test gives a p-value of 0.03.
Is the result statistically significant, at the 5% level?
Yes!
0.03 is below 0.05. But it's still not a 3% chance that the null is true.
Next: what happens when a test gets it wrong? Type 1 and Type 2 errors.
